---
title: "Population coefficients and group variation"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

We have already seen the [crossed units](structured-data.qmd) in the MALD trial table: participants respond to many spoken words, and words receive responses from many participants. We now need a model that can answer two questions at once. First, what is the average association between lexical frequency and response time across the population we want to study? Second, how much do particular listeners and words depart from that average relation?

Recall the measurements. [MALD](multiple-regression.qmd) records onset-to-response time, acoustic duration, SUBTLEX frequency, and trial order, and the [response transformation](response-transformations.qmd) explains why we take the logarithm of response time. Fixing those meanings before we build the model prevents a coefficient from drifting away from the measurement it is meant to summarize.

The model uses [variance, covariance, and standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) to describe group deviations and their relations. Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) applies only after the shared deviations are supplied. A [residual](residuals.qmd) is the observed response minus its fitted value. Participant and item effects therefore require raw repeated MALD trials; they cannot be recovered from one mean per word.

The basic idea is to begin with one shared regression line and then allow sampled listeners and words to depart from it. We first work through that idea with one predictor, then write the compact notation used by the full model.

When we refer to listener and word populations below, we mean the exchangeable
distributions specified by the model. The retained MALD listeners and words were
not drawn as probability samples. Extending the fitted variation beyond the
represented listeners and items therefore depends on the assumption that these
model distributions provide a useful account of the new listeners and words we
care about.

## Beginning with the scientific target

Begin with log frequency alone. If the population intercept is $\beta_0$ and the population frequency coefficient is $\beta_f$, the shared relation is

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid x_i]=\beta_0+\beta_f x_i.
$$

Here $Y_i$ is log response time on trial $i$, and $x_i$ is standardized log frequency for the spoken word on that trial. A negative $\beta_f$ means that expected log response time decreases as frequency increases; a positive value means that it increases. This coefficient describes the shared relation before we ask whether a particular listener is generally faster or slower.

The full analysis also contains standardized log acoustic duration and standardized trial order. Recall that [standardizing a variable](centering-predictors.qmd) subtracts its sample mean and divides by its sample standard deviation. We can collect the intercept and these three predictor values in a row vector $\mathbf x_i$, and collect their coefficients in a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$. Their matrix product is shorthand for the familiar sum

$$
\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
=\beta_0+\beta_f x_i^{(f)}+\beta_d x_i^{(d)}+\beta_t x_i^{(t)}.
$$

This is the same [design matrix notation](design-matrices.qmd) used for multiple regression: multiplication pairs each predictor value with its coefficient and adds the products. With group deviations included, the population relation becomes

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\mathbf b]
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b.
$$

Here $\boldsymbol\beta$ contains the population intercept and the three population associations. The second product, $\mathbf z_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b$, selects and adds the participant and word deviations that belong to trial $i$. In particular, $\beta_{\text{frequency}}$ is the expected change in log response time for a one standard deviation increase in log frequency, holding duration and trial order fixed.

Here one standard deviation is computed from the retained correct trial table used to fit the model. If $s_f$ is that sample standard deviation, then $z_{fi}=(x_{fi}-\bar x_f)/s_f$. Thus a one unit change in `z_frequency` means an $s_f$ unit change in original log frequency rather than one raw frequency unit. In a prediction study, the centering and scale constants should be estimated on training data and carried into assessment data.

The word *fixed* does not mean known, measured without uncertainty, or constant across every conceivable population. It means that the coefficient is not itself indexed by a grouping level in this model.

## Representing sampled variation

For a particular participant $p$, an intercept deviation $b_{0p}$ represents a persistent shift from the population center. A slope deviation $b_{1p}$ represents the difference between that participant's frequency association and the population association. The participant's line is

$$
(\beta_0+b_{0p})+(\beta_f+b_{1p})x_i^{(f)}.
$$

The actual values are estimated from all listeners together. For participant $p$, collect the two deviations in a vector:

$$
\mathbf b_p=
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0p}\\b_{1p}\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_p).
$$

The symbol $\boldsymbol\Sigma_p$ is a **covariance matrix**. Its diagonal entries record the variance of participant intercepts and slopes, while its off-diagonal entries record whether faster or slower baselines tend to accompany larger or smaller frequency associations. This extends the scalar [variance and covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) ideas by arranging those quantities in a table.

Word $w$ receives an intercept deviation,

$$
c_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),
$$

and the trial residual is

$$
\varepsilon_{pwi}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

Combining the pieces gives

$$
Y_{pwi}
=\beta_0+\beta_f x_{wi}^{(f)}+\beta_d x_{wi}^{(d)}
+\beta_t x_{pwi}^{(t)}
+b_{0p}+b_{1p}x_{wi}^{(f)}+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi}.
$$

The grouping terms follow the participant-by-word incidence structure. A participant intercept represents persistent listener speed; a word intercept represents repeated lexical-item difficulty. A participant frequency slope is requested because each participant hears words spanning frequency values and the scientific target generalizes the frequency association across listeners. An item frequency slope is not requested because a word's lexical frequency is constant across repetitions of that word. The Gaussian response and residual assumptions concern log response time conditional on these terms, and the participant, word, and residual components are assumed mutually independent unless a covariance is written explicitly.

The frequency column and participant identifier both enter the construction of the linear predictor, but they have different roles. Frequency is a measured predictor with a population coefficient. Participant identity indexes deviations drawn from a population distribution.

## From the conditional model to the marginal likelihood {#gaussian-mixed-model-likelihood}

How do we estimate the population coefficients and the variances of the group
deviations? The conditional equation above describes the response after the
participant and word deviations have been supplied. But those deviations are
unobserved. The likelihood for the observed responses must average over their
normal distributions.

Stack the trial responses in a vector $\mathbf y$, the population predictor rows
in a matrix $\mathbf X$, and the participant and word predictor rows in a matrix
$\mathbf Z$. Collect all group deviations in $\mathbf b$. The model becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf b
&\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf Z\mathbf b,
\sigma^2\mathbf I),\\
\mathbf b
&\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf G_{\boldsymbol\theta}).
\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $\mathbf G_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ contains the participant and word
variances and covariances. We will use $\boldsymbol\theta$ for those covariance
parameters together with the residual variance. Conditional independence gives
the normal density $p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf b,\boldsymbol\beta,
\boldsymbol\theta)$. Averaging that density over the possible group deviations
gives the **marginal likelihood**:

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta;\mathbf y)
=
\int
p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf b,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
p(\mathbf b\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
\,d\mathbf b.
$$

For a Gaussian mixed model, this integral has a closed form. The group
deviations contribute $\mathbf Z\mathbf G_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}$
to the response covariance, while trial residuals contribute
$\sigma^2\mathbf I$. We can see both contributions by calculating the marginal
mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf Y]
&=
\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf Z\mathbb{E}[\mathbf b]
+\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol\varepsilon]
=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\\[4pt]
\operatorname{Var}[\mathbf Y]
&=
\mathbf Z\operatorname{Var}[\mathbf b]\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}
+\operatorname{Var}[\boldsymbol\varepsilon]\\
&=
\mathbf Z\mathbf G_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}
+\sigma^2\mathbf I.
\end{aligned}
$$

The variance sum uses the assumed independence of $\mathbf b$ and
$\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. A linear combination of jointly Gaussian variables
is Gaussian. Thus

$$
\mathbf Y
\sim
\mathcal N(
\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}),
\qquad
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}
=
\mathbf Z\mathbf G_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T}
+\sigma^2\mathbf I.
$$

This covariance is where the repeated units enter the likelihood. Two rows that
share a participant or word receive a nonzero covariance through the appropriate
columns of $\mathbf Z$. In the expression below,
$|\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}|$ is the **determinant**, a single number that
records the volume implied by the covariance, and
$\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}$ is the matrix inverse that rescales
residual differences by that covariance.

The full marginal log likelihood is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
&=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac12\log|\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}|\\
&\quad
-\frac12
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta).
\end{aligned}
$$

The final quadratic measures residual distance after accounting for the fitted
covariance. A derivative records how the log likelihood changes under a small
change in a parameter. If we hold $\boldsymbol\theta$ fixed and take one
derivative for each entry of $\boldsymbol\beta$, the resulting collection is
the **score**. At an interior maximum it equals zero, giving

$$
\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
=\mathbf 0.
$$

When the columns of $\mathbf X$ are linearly independent, no column can be
constructed as a weighted sum of the others. Under this condition the required
inverse exists, and the solution is the
**generalized least squares (GLS)** estimate

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\boldsymbol\theta}
=
(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}\mathbf y.
$$

The basic idea is familiar from ordinary least squares. We are still choosing
coefficients by a weighted squared discrepancy. The inverse covariance gives
less weight to directions with greater modeled variation and prevents repeated
rows from being treated as independent copies.

The covariance score shows why the remaining estimates require a search. Let
$\mathbf V_k=\partial\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}/\partial\theta_k$ be the
change in the response covariance produced by a small change in covariance
parameter $\theta_k$, and let
$\mathbf r=\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$. We will also use
$\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf A)$, the **trace** of a square matrix $\mathbf A$,
which means the sum of its diagonal entries. Holding the population
coefficients fixed, we use two matrix derivative identities:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_k}\log|\mathbf V|
=
\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf V_k),
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathbf V^{-1}}{\partial\theta_k}
=
-\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf V_k\mathbf V^{-1}.
$$

The first identity differentiates the log determinant. The second says that an
increase in covariance produces the corresponding decrease in precision.
Applying the first identity to the determinant term and the second to the
quadratic term gives

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta_k}
=
-\frac12\operatorname{tr}
(\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}\mathbf V_k)
+\frac12
\mathbf r^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}
\mathbf V_k
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}\mathbf r.
$$

The first term charges for increasing the volume of the fitted covariance; the
second rewards a covariance change when it better accommodates the residual
pattern. Substituting the GLS estimate into the likelihood gives
the same profiled score because the coefficient score is zero at that estimate.

The variance and covariance parameters generally have no closed form. For each
candidate $\boldsymbol\theta$, `lmer()` finds the corresponding GLS coefficient
vector and evaluates a profiled objective. A numerical optimizer then searches
over the remaining covariance parameters. The search reported below uses
`bobyqa`, which proposes new parameter values from a local quadratic
approximation while respecting the nonnegative variance constraints.

### Maximum likelihood and restricted maximum likelihood

There are two related objectives in common use. **Maximum likelihood (ML)**
maximizes the marginal log likelihood above over both
$\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\boldsymbol\theta$. **Restricted maximum likelihood
(REML)** first removes the $p$ population coefficient directions and then
estimates the covariance parameters from the remaining $n-p$ response
directions. To make “removes” concrete, choose an $n\times(n-p)$ matrix
$\mathbf A$ whose columns satisfy $\mathbf A^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X=\mathbf 0$.
Then $\mathbf A^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Y$ has mean zero and covariance
$\mathbf A^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf A$, so its
likelihood contains no $\boldsymbol\beta$. Different valid choices of
$\mathbf A$ lead to the same covariance estimates. Writing that likelihood in
terms of the original response gives, up to a parameter independent constant,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{\mathrm R}(\boldsymbol\theta)
&=
-\frac12\Bigl[
(n-p)\log(2\pi)
+\log|\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}|\\
&\qquad
+\log|\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}\mathbf X|
+\mathbf y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf y
\Bigr],
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
=
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}
-
\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}\mathbf X
(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-1}.
$$

This is the covariance-weighted version of the earlier [projection into fitted
and residual directions](design-matrices.qmd#fig-projection-fitted-residual).
Using the same determinant and inverse identities as above, together with

$$
\frac{\partial\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta}}
{\partial\theta_k}
=
-\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf V_k
\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta},
$$

we can differentiate each term of the restricted objective. The covariance
score is

$$
\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm R}}{\partial\theta_k}
=
-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf V_k)
+\frac12
\mathbf y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\mathbf V_k\mathbf P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mathbf y.
$$

The optimizer searches for covariance parameters that make these score
components approximately zero, subject to the requirement that the fitted
covariance matrices remain valid.

Why introduce a second objective? In an ordinary linear regression with Gaussian errors, ML uses
$\operatorname{SSE}/n$ for the residual variance, while removing the $p$ fitted
coefficient directions gives $\operatorname{SSE}/(n-p)$. REML generalizes that
degrees of freedom correction to the covariance parameters of a mixed model.
There is no single replacement denominator once several participant and word
variance components enter $\mathbf V_{\boldsymbol\theta}$; the determinant and
quadratic terms perform the correction together.

A potential worry is that REML gives a likelihood for comparing any two mixed
models. The restricted objective depends on the columns of $\mathbf X$, so REML
values from models with different population predictors are not directly
comparable. We use ML for likelihood comparisons that change those predictors.
REML remains useful for estimating covariance components when the population
predictor structure is held fixed.

## Fitting the MALD model

The function `lmer()` fits the Gaussian mixed model. Its formula reads from left to right: `log_rt` is the response; the terms before the first grouping expression receive population coefficients; `(1 + z_frequency | participant_id)` gives each participant an intercept and frequency slope deviation; and `(1 | item)` gives each word an intercept deviation. The helper function `standardize()` below uses `scale()` to subtract a column's mean and divide by its standard deviation. We request REML explicitly. Finally, `maxfun` raises the number of objective evaluations available to `bobyqa`.

```{r}
#| label: mald-fixed-random
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

standardize <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(scale(x))
}

mald$z_frequency <- standardize(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$z_duration <- standardize(mald$log_duration)
mald$z_trial <- standardize(mald$trial_order)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = lmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

data.frame(
  term = names(lme4::fixef(fit)),
  estimate = unname(lme4::fixef(fit)),
  row.names = NULL
)

participant_deviations <- ranef(fit)$participant_id
example_participant <- rownames(participant_deviations)[[1L]]
data.frame(
  participant_id = example_participant,
  population_intercept = fixef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]],
  fitted_intercept_deviation =
    participant_deviations[example_participant, "(Intercept)"],
  population_frequency_slope = fixef(fit)[["z_frequency"]],
  fitted_frequency_slope_deviation =
    participant_deviations[example_participant, "z_frequency"]
)
```

The full MALD covariance is large because there is one row per retained trial.
To check the likelihood algebra directly, we take the one hundred words with the
most retained responses and keep every observed participant response to those
words. We then fit an intercept-only group structure to that subtable. This
keeps the covariance matrix small enough to display every operation while
preserving repeated words and the participants who supplied the responses.

The calculation uses a **Cholesky factor** to evaluate the covariance
determinant. For a positive definite covariance matrix, `chol()` finds an upper
triangular matrix $\mathbf R$ satisfying
$\mathbf V=\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}\mathbf R$. The determinant of a triangular
matrix is the product of its diagonal entries, so
$\log|\mathbf V|=2\sum_j\log R_{jj}$. This factorization avoids expanding a
large determinant term by term. The call to `stopifnot()` at the end halts the
calculation if either direct result differs from `lmer()` by more than the stated
numerical tolerance.

```{r}
#| label: check-mald-marginal-likelihood

item_counts <- sort(table(mald$item), decreasing = TRUE)
selected_items <- names(head(item_counts, 100L))
mald_check <- mald[mald$item %in% selected_items, ]

check_fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 | participant_id) + (1 | item),
  data = mald_check,
  REML = FALSE
)

X_check <- model.matrix(check_fit)
y_check <- model.response(model.frame(check_fit))
Z_participant <- model.matrix(
  ~ 0 + factor(participant_id),
  data = mald_check
)
Z_item <- model.matrix(~ 0 + factor(item), data = mald_check)
check_variances <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(check_fit))
tau_participant2 <- check_variances$vcov[
  check_variances$grp == "participant_id" &
    is.na(check_variances$var2)
]
tau_item2 <- check_variances$vcov[
  check_variances$grp == "item" & is.na(check_variances$var2)
]
sigma2_check <- sigma(check_fit)^2

V_check <-
  tau_participant2 * tcrossprod(Z_participant) +
  tau_item2 * tcrossprod(Z_item) +
  sigma2_check * diag(nrow(mald_check))
V_inverse_X <- solve(V_check, X_check)
V_inverse_y <- solve(V_check, y_check)
beta_gls <- solve(
  crossprod(X_check, V_inverse_X),
  crossprod(X_check, V_inverse_y)
)
check_residual <- y_check - drop(X_check %*% beta_gls)
V_cholesky <- chol(V_check)
log_determinant_V <- 2 * sum(log(diag(V_cholesky)))
log_likelihood_direct <- -.5 * (
  nrow(mald_check) * log(2 * pi) +
    log_determinant_V +
    crossprod(check_residual, solve(V_check, check_residual))
)

stopifnot(
  max(abs(drop(beta_gls) - fixef(check_fit))) < 1e-7,
  abs(drop(log_likelihood_direct) - as.numeric(logLik(check_fit))) < 1e-6
)

data.frame(
  observed_trials = nrow(mald_check),
  observed_participants = length(unique(mald_check$participant_id)),
  observed_words = length(unique(mald_check$item)),
  direct_log_likelihood = drop(log_likelihood_direct),
  lmer_log_likelihood = as.numeric(logLik(check_fit)),
  largest_gls_coefficient_difference =
    max(abs(drop(beta_gls) - fixef(check_fit)))
)
```

The direct calculation uses the fitted covariance parameters and recovers both
the GLS population coefficients and the ML log likelihood reported by `lmer()`.
Thus the software output instantiates the marginal Gaussian likelihood rather
than introducing a separate estimation rule.

The second table instantiates the earlier equation with one observed MALD participant. Adding each fitted deviation to its population coefficient gives that participant's fitted intercept and frequency slope.

The formula maps term by term onto the mathematical model:

| `lmer` term | Mathematical role |
|---|---|
| `z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial` | population coefficients $\beta_f,\beta_d,\beta_t$ |
| `(1 + z_frequency \| participant_id)` | correlated participant deviations $(b_{0p},b_{1p})$ |
| `(1 \| item)` | word intercept $c_w$ |
| implicit Gaussian residual | $\varepsilon_{pwi}$ |

The optimizer settings address computation. Changing them does not change the probability model or create support for a grouping term that the design cannot estimate.

The fitted frequency coefficient is `r sprintf("%.3f", lme4::fixef(fit)[["z_frequency"]])` log response time units per standard deviation. This is a population association conditional on duration and trial order. It neither describes one particular participant's slope nor establishes a causal effect of lexical frequency.

## Showing raw data and the fitted population relation

Plotting all trials would obscure the relation. We thus summarize the raw responses in empirical frequency bins and draw the fitted population line at mean duration and mean trial order.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-fixed-random
frequency_breaks <- unique(quantile(
  mald$z_frequency,
  probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 13L),
  names = FALSE
))
mald$frequency_bin <- cut(
  mald$z_frequency,
  breaks = frequency_breaks,
  include.lowest = TRUE
)

raw_bins <- aggregate(
  cbind(z_frequency, log_rt) ~ frequency_bin,
  data = mald,
  FUN = mean
)

prediction_grid <- data.frame(
  z_frequency = seq(
    min(raw_bins$z_frequency),
    max(raw_bins$z_frequency),
    length.out = 160L
  ),
  z_duration = 0,
  z_trial = 0
)
prediction_grid$fitted_log_rt <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = prediction_grid,
  re.form = NA
)

ggplot(raw_bins, aes(x = z_frequency, y = log_rt)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey35", size = 1.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = prediction_grid,
    aes(y = fitted_log_rt),
    color = "#1F5A85",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "SUBTLEX log frequency (standardized)",
    y = "Log response time"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The points are raw bin means. The line sets participant and item deviations to zero, so it describes the fitted population relation on the same response scale. An observed participant or word generally receives an additional fitted deviation.

## Storage type does not determine modeling role

Frequency, participant, item, and part of speech can all be stored as columns. Their storage types do not decide whether they receive population coefficients or group distributions. The decision follows the estimand and sampling design. A measured property that encodes a theoretical contrast belongs in the population relation. A sampled identifier that records repeated observations can index remaining variation around that relation.

We fit frequency, acoustic duration, and trial order because those terms let us isolate the participant and word covariance calculation. Tucker et al. analyze additional controls, so the coefficient comparison here answers a narrower question.

## Recap and check

1. Why is there a participant frequency slope but no item frequency slope? Frequency varies within participants but is constant within each word.
2. Does “fixed effect” mean known without uncertainty? No. It is an estimated population coefficient that is not indexed by a grouping level in this model.

We next work through how these shared group distributions produce [partial pooling](random-effects.qmd).
